Follow the YAML specification below when answering.

instructions: 'Prompt version: article-claims-v2.


  You extract atomic claims from one article so a person can fact-check them later.
  You do not search, and you do not assign a verdict.


  Return only JSON:

  {"claims":[{"id":"c1","source_quote":"exact substring of the article","normalized_claim":"one
  standalone claim","category":"checkable_fact|opinion|prediction|needs_context","missing_context":[],"verification_scope":"external_fact|document_content|text_analysis"}]}


  Rules:

  - source_quote must be copied character for character from the article. Do not fix
  spelling, and do not join text from two places.

  - Split a sentence that states two independent facts into two claims. Each quote
  must still be an exact substring.

  - Keep limiters in normalized_claim: some, all, only, may, as of a date, a named
  exam, a team, a tier, or a price category.

  - Preserve the source quote''s asserted meaning in normalized_claim: keep its subject,
  action, polarity, tense, certainty, time, quantities, and scope. Do not weaken a
  forecast into a present fact, strengthen a possibility into certainty, reverse a
  negation, or omit a limiting phrase. If a faithful normalization is unclear, use
  the source wording and explain the missing context.

  - Extract statements about the limits of current knowledge as claims too. Phrases
  such as "unknown," "unclear," "not known," or "no data" assert a state of knowledge;
  do not omit them or turn them into a claim that an event or object did not exist.
  Preserve whose knowledge is limited, which aspect is unknown, and any stated time
  or scope.

  - Do not add ordinal or superlative limits such as “first,” “earliest,” or “only”
  unless the quote or one clear context explicitly states them. Never turn an unordered
  event into a first event.

  - In normalized_claim, resolve a pronoun or demonstrative such as "it", "they",
  "these actions", "that exam", "the same report", "the paper", or "that date" from
  the article context only when there is one clear antecedent. Preserve the source
  quote exactly. If the antecedent is ambiguous or absent, keep the claim cautious
  and list the missing referent in missing_context; never guess.

  - Do not replace a claim with a neighboring sentence while resolving context. The
  normalized claim must preserve the source quote''s subject, predicate, numbers,
  and direction. If the quote is "These actions allowed X to flourish", do not turn
  it into a claim about how a release was licensed. Keep the causal assertion and
  list any unclear action, concrete outcome or measure, and causal basis in missing_context.

  - For causal language such as "caused", "allowed", "enabled", "led to", or "resulted
  in", check whether the article names the action, outcome, and a concrete indicator.
  Vague outcomes such as "flourish" or "improve" need the missing object or measure
  and evidence for the causal link listed in missing_context. Do not treat temporal
  order alone as causal proof.

  - When a claim reports that headlines or another speaker described a gain, improvement,
  score, or other result with a comparison, preserve that attribution and identify
  the result or measure being described. If the article does not make the referent
  clear, include it in missing_context instead of guessing.

  - If the article attributes the statement, keep that attribution in source_quote
  and in normalized_claim. Phrases to keep include "the report says", "the authors
  add", "according to", "I think", and "headlines called". Do not turn an attributed
  statement into a bare fact.

  - Keep a statement''s existing speaker, source, role, and attribution verb when
  the article supplies them. If the attribution is outside quotation marks or is carried
  by a clearly connected continuation, make source_quote one exact contiguous substring
  that includes the statement and enough attribution context; keep the same attribution
  in normalized_claim. Do not infer a speaker or source when the article leaves it
  unclear.

  - Do not extend an attribution across "and". "The report says A, and B" supports
  "The report says A". It does not support "The report says B". Leave B as its own
  claim without that attribution.

  - Preserve semantic relationships between the subject, action, object, and any necessary
  participants. Keep stated spatial and directional relationships (for example, which
  place or object is inside, beside, connected to, or leads to another), as well as
  causal direction. When splitting independent facts, make each claim''s quote and
  normalization retain the relationship needed to understand that fact; do not keep
  only a measurement or outcome while dropping the action or connection that gives
  it meaning.

  - Preserve appositive definitions and relationships that identify a place or entity,
  likelihood qualifiers such as "rarer", "alternatively", and "usually", and qualifications
  about a speaker''s role or independence. A quote must begin at a sentence or clause
  boundary that retains these qualifiers. For a continued quotation, carry the speaker
  only when the article makes the continuation explicit in the same paragraph; otherwise
  list the missing speaker in missing_context without guessing.

  - Include checkable method, data, and sample facts, including data spans, sample
  sizes, and model inputs when stated. Keep each as a source-grounded claim; do not
  add details the article does not state.

  - A price claim needs the named product or service being billed. Fill that name
  only when the price clause in the article states it. If it does not, list the missing
  product or service in missing_context. Do not borrow a name from the other half
  of an "and" sentence.

  - missing_context names a gap in what that claim asserts. A claim that headlines
  used a phrase needs the headline, not proof that the phrase''s comparison is true.

  - verification_scope is document_content when the claim is about what one resolved
  document says, lists, does not say, or does not report. It is text_analysis when
  the sentence classifies another line as a forecast, preference, or opinion. Otherwise
  it is external_fact.

  - If a sentence says a line is a forecast or a preference, and then says it is not
  in the report, return those as two claims.

  - "on purpose", "deliberately", and "meant to" are intention, not opinion. "I think",
  "best", and "worst" are opinion.

  - Do not guess which document a pronoun or "the document" names. Leave it unresolved
  when more than one document is possible.

  - checkable_fact: a statement about a date, number, name, price, policy, or result
  that could be checked against a source.

  - opinion: the writer''s evaluation. Do not call it a fact.

  - prediction: a claim about the future. Do not call it a fact.

  - needs_context: use this category only when the claim''s own subject, date, or
  baseline is missing. Name that gap in missing_context.

  - Do not drop a checkable fact because it is narrow. Do not invent claims that the
  article does not state.


  If repair_errors is not empty, the previous quotes failed those checks. Return a
  full replacement whose source_quote values occur in the article.

  '

{"article": "Rubio says there's 'zero' information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor
November 18, 2026 3:27 AM ET By The Associated Press
MANILA, Philippines — Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's "zero" information that the cascade of service outages, which snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications, are related to each other or to a malign actor.
Rubio sought to calm Americans as he traveled with President Donald Trump and they prepared to leave the Philippines for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the tech hub of Shenzhen, China.
"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.
In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for disruptions — and even staunch Trump allies have accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause.
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage on Tuesday.
"It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine," Trump said in Manila, declaring that "things like that happen."
But as concern mounted, Rubio appeared to publicly address American worries from the other side of the world.
There has been a steady stream of outages this week
Trump's nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages was an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.
The series of outages began Thursday, when Microsoft's email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to "an earlier network capacity upgrade."
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by "a software bug" and was "not cyber-related."
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as "routine maintenance."
Trump's nonchalance was not shared by some of his allies
Earlier Tuesday, Karoline Leavitt, Trump's former press secretary, said the White House needed to do more to explain the situation.
"What I would say to the White House is: transparency is key," Leavitt said on Fox News. Later on social media, she praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network.
"Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyberattack incident," Clayton said, explaining that the U.S. government believes the incidents were caused by security upgrades that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump's Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical of the lack of information from the federal government.
"Americans aren't stupid," she posted on social media. "We want and deserve to know what's really going on."
Meghan McCain, a conservative commentator who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, voiced similar concerns.
"Someone high in the administration needs to get on TV and tell the American people NOW what is going on," McCain, who is also the daughter of late GOP Sen. John McCain, wrote on X. "No one who lived through COVID is believing this is all a coincidence."
After Trump and other administration officials failed to offer reassurance on those cascading tech problems, Rubio seemed to take on the role of reassurer-in-chief when he appeared unexpectedly in Manila to take questions. The secretary of state is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, though he lately has declined to comment on whether he would consider a campaign to try to succeed Trump.
But Trump's role in the immediate moment was a pressing concern, even for supporters in his Make America Great Again movement.
"Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyberattack," Laura Loomer, a right-wing personality known for her incendiary social media presence, wrote on X. "President Trump should come back to the United States." She did not present any evidence of an attack.
Conservative commentator Kylie Jane Kremer, writing on X, demanded accountability. "And why does it feel like we're being told everything is fine while the very systems our country depends on are experiencing serious failures?" she said.", "repair_errors": []}

{"article": "Rubio says there's 'zero' information that U.S. outages are caused by a malign actor
November 18, 2026 3:27 AM ET By The Associated Press
MANILA, Philippines — Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's "zero" information that the cascade of service outages, which snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications, are related to each other or to a malign actor.
Rubio sought to calm Americans as he traveled with President Donald Trump and they prepared to leave the Philippines for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the tech hub of Shenzhen, China.
"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.
In recent days, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected by technical failures and outages. Trump has faced a groundswell of criticism as friends and foes alike said the White House must answer for disruptions — and even staunch Trump allies have accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause.
Trump was dismissive when asked whether he was concerned about the Chase outage on Tuesday.
"It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine," Trump said in Manila, declaring that "things like that happen."
But as concern mounted, Rubio appeared to publicly address American worries from the other side of the world.
There has been a steady stream of outages this week
Trump's nonchalance was not shared by those already distrustful of the government and big institutions. And for Americans across the political spectrum, the drip-drip-drip of alarming and frustrating outages was an unsettling reminder of perils posed by interconnected tech networks.
The series of outages began Thursday, when Microsoft's email and other tools went down, paralyzing millions of workers who rely on them. Microsoft traced the issue to "an earlier network capacity upgrade."
Flights across the country were grounded the next day in the longest so-called ground stop since 9/11. The Federal Aviation Administration blamed a router upgrade.
By Monday, the banks were in the spotlight, as customers reported difficulty accessing online accounts at several major financial institutions and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system. Chase said it was caused by "a software bug" and was "not cyber-related."
The same day, United Airlines said it had resolved an internal system outage that delayed departing flights.
And on Tuesday, an internal network that the National Security Agency uses to communicate classified information was offline after what the agency described as "routine maintenance."
Trump's nonchalance was not shared by some of his allies
Earlier Tuesday, Karoline Leavitt, Trump's former press secretary, said the White House needed to do more to explain the situation.
"What I would say to the White House is: transparency is key," Leavitt said on Fox News. Later on social media, she praised the White House for having Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton address the outages in an interview on Fox Business Network.
"Looking very diligently across the landscape, we are not seeing this as a cyberattack incident," Clayton said, explaining that the U.S. government believes the incidents were caused by security upgrades that took longer than planned or encountered unexpected hiccups.
Tricia McLaughlin, a former spokesperson for Trump's Department of Homeland Security, was skeptical of the lack of information from the federal government.
"Americans aren't stupid," she posted on social media. "We want and deserve to know what's really going on."
Meghan McCain, a conservative commentator who is sometimes at odds with Trump and his allies, voiced similar concerns.
"Someone high in the administration needs to get on TV and tell the American people NOW what is going on," McCain, who is also the daughter of late GOP Sen. John McCain, wrote on X. "No one who lived through COVID is believing this is all a coincidence."
After Trump and other administration officials failed to offer reassurance on those cascading tech problems, Rubio seemed to take on the role of reassurer-in-chief when he appeared unexpectedly in Manila to take questions. The secretary of state is seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, though he lately has declined to comment on whether he would consider a campaign to try to succeed Trump.
But Trump's role in the immediate moment was a pressing concern, even for supporters in his Make America Great Again movement.
"Our leaders are lying to us. This is very clearly a coordinated cyberattack," Laura Loomer, a right-wing personality known for her incendiary social media presence, wrote on X. "President Trump should come back to the United States." She did not present any evidence of an attack.
